title: Zero article with uncountable and plural nouns
description: Do not use 'a/an' or 'the' before general uncountable nouns or plural nouns when referring to the concept in general.

title: Definite article with specific reference
description: Use 'the' when both writer and reader know which specific thing is being referred to — typically on second mention, or when there is only one of the thing.

wrong: A government should invest in education. A government also...
correct: A government should invest in education. The government also...

title: No article before proper nouns and most country names
description: Do not use 'the' before most country names, continents, cities, or people's names. Exceptions: the USA, the UK, the Philippines.

title: Simple past for completed events in IELTS Task 1
description: When describing data at a fixed point in the past, use the simple past tense, not the present or present perfect.

wrong: The figure reaches a peak in 2010
correct: The figure reached a peak in 2010

title: Present simple for timeless facts and opinions
description: Use the present simple to state general truths, ongoing situations without a time anchor, or the writer's opinion.

wrong: Education played a crucial role in development
Governments had a duty to protect citizens
correct: Education plays a crucial role in development
Governments have a duty to protect citizens

title: Future forms for predictions and trends
description: Use 'will + verb', 'is likely to', or 'is expected to' for predictions. Avoid the present simple for future reference without a time adverb.

wrong: The population increases to 10 billion by 2050
correct: The population will increase to 10 billion by 2050
The population is expected to reach 10 billion by 2050

title: Singular verb after 'the number of'
description: 'The number of + plural noun' takes a singular verb. Compare with 'a number of + plural noun', which takes a plural verb.

wrong: The number of students are increasing
The number of cars have risen
correct: The number of students is increasing
A number of cars have been recalled

title: Verb agreement with collective and abstract nouns
description: Abstract nouns (government, society, data, research) and collective nouns are usually singular in IELTS academic writing.

wrong: The data show that crime are rising
correct: The data show that crime is rising

title: Adjective + preposition fixed collocations
description: Many adjectives require a fixed preposition. Memorise the most common: interested IN, responsible FOR, dependent ON, associated WITH, concerned ABOUT, related TO.

title: Verb + preposition fixed collocations
description: Common verb-preposition pairs to memorise: contribute TO, invest IN, depend ON, focus ON, lead TO, result IN, consist OF, differ FROM.

title: Noun vs. verb form after modal and auxiliary verbs
description: After modal verbs (can, should, must, will) and after 'to', always use the base verb form — not a noun or adjective.

wrong: policies can a reduction of crime
we need to the improvement of

title: Correct derivational form (noun/verb/adjective/adverb)
description: Each word family has distinct suffixes. Using the wrong form is a common lexical error: economy (n) / economic (adj) / economically (adv) / economise (v).

title: Avoiding the 'Although…, but…' double connector error
description: A clause beginning with 'although', 'while', 'even though' is subordinate — it cannot also use 'but', 'however', or 'yet' as a second connector in the same sentence.

wrong: Although the economy grew, but unemployment remained high
While wages rose, however living costs also increased
correct: Although the economy grew, unemployment remained high
While wages rose, living costs also increased

title: Avoiding run-on sentences and comma splices
description: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a coordinating conjunction (and, but, so, yet).

wrong: Crime increased sharply, the government introduced new laws
The graph shows a rise, it then falls in 2015
correct: Crime increased sharply, so the government introduced new laws
The graph shows a rise; it then falls in 2015

title: Comma after sentence-initial adverbials
description: When a sentence begins with a conjunctive adverb (However, Therefore, Furthermore, In addition, As a result, Nevertheless), it must be followed by a comma.

title: Uncountable nouns that cannot be pluralised
description: These common IELTS nouns have no plural form: information, advice, research, evidence, knowledge, furniture, equipment, money, traffic, homework, news, progress.

title: Irregular plurals and always-plural nouns
description: Some nouns have irregular plurals (criterion/criteria, phenomenon/phenomena, medium/media). Some are always plural (police, people, cattle).

title: Verb-noun collocations: 'make' vs 'do' vs 'take'
description: Common verb-noun collocations are fixed. Mistakes with make/do/take/have are frequent in IELTS essays.

title: Adjective-noun collocations: strong vs heavy vs high
description: Many adjective-noun pairings are fixed in English. 'Strong', 'heavy', and 'high' are commonly confused.

title: Pronoun-antecedent agreement and reference clarity
description: A pronoun must clearly refer to one specific noun and agree with it in number and gender. Avoid vague 'they' or 'it' when the referent is unclear.

wrong: The government said they would reduce taxes
When a student fails, they are blamed by teachers, who they rarely acknowledge
correct: The government said it would reduce taxes

title: Avoiding dangling and misplaced modifiers
description: A participial phrase at the start of a sentence must describe the subject of the main clause. If it does not, the result is a dangling modifier.

wrong: Being a developing country, the economy faces many challenges
Having studied the graph, a clear trend can be seen
correct: Being a developing country, Vietnam faces many economic challenges
Having studied the graph, we can see a clear trend

title: Double comparatives and superlatives
description: Never combine 'more/most' with an '-er/-est' adjective. Use one or the other.

title: Parallel structure in comparisons
description: When comparing two things with 'as…as' or 'than', both sides must be grammatically parallel. Also avoid 'as…than' and 'more…as'.

wrong: the rate in 2020 is higher than 2015
China's rate compared to it rose faster than India
correct: the rate in 2020 is higher than that in 2015

title: Relative clause punctuation: defining vs non-defining
description: A defining relative clause (no commas) identifies which one. A non-defining relative clause (with commas) adds extra information about an already-identified noun.

wrong: The country, that has the highest rate, should act
Students who they study abroad gain more skills
correct: The country that has the highest rate should act
The country, which has the highest rate, should act (non-defining)
Students who study abroad gain more skills

title: Past perfect for events before another past event
description: Use the past perfect (had + past participle) when describing an event that occurred before another event in the past. Do not use simple past for both.

wrong: Before the policy changed, crime increased significantly
correct: By 2015, the rate had already peaked
Before the policy changed, crime had increased significantly

title: Time and place prepositions: at / in / on
description: Use AT for specific times and places (at 5pm, at school). Use IN for months, years, seasons, countries, cities. Use ON for days and dates.
